title: Bài sưu tầm 104 - Passage 1: The Terracotta Army: Ancient Guardians in Clay
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 1 — TEST 104

The Terracotta Army: Ancient Guardians in Clay

Paragraph 1. In March 1974, during a period of severe drought, a group of local farmers was digging a subterranean well approximately 30 kilometres east of the ancient capital of Xi’an in Shaanxi province, China. While excavating through dry soil several metres down, their shovels struck hard, baked clay. Pushing further, they unearthed terracotta pottery shards, followed by bronze arrowheads and a life-sized sculpted human head. Recognizing the potential significance of the finds, local officials notified provincial authorities, summoning archaeological teams to investigate the terrain. What began as a routine water well excavation swiftly transformed into one of the most astonishing archaeological discoveries of the twentieth century: the Terracotta Army of Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor of unified China.

Paragraph 2. Qin Shi Huang conquered six rival kingdoms to unify the Chinese empire in 221 BCE. Believing he would continue his autocratic rule in the afterlife, the emperor commissioned the construction of a colossal subterranean necropolis shortly after ascending the throne as a teenager. Imperial historical annals written a century later by the Han dynasty historian Sima Qian chronicled that over 700,000 forced laborers and skilled craftsmen toiled for nearly four decades to build the imperial tomb complex. The underground city, spanning several square kilometres, was filled with palaces, sacrificial pits, and models of the cosmos, protected by an infantry vanguard of thousands of life-sized terracotta soldiers, archers, charioteers, and horses arranged in strict military formations.

Paragraph 3. Archaeological excavations revealed that the creation of the army was a triumph of ancient mass assembly and logistical organization. Government workshops operated an early system of modular manufacturing. Craftsmen used coarse, local clay to press core body segments—feet, legs, torsos, and arms—out of reusable hollow moulds. However, instead of producing uniform, clone-like figures, artists individually sculpted unique facial expressions, distinctive hairstyles, and realistic ear shapes onto each warrior by hand. Every soldier was cast with individualized features representing diverse ethnic groups within the newly unified realm. Master craftsmen stamped their personal names onto hidden sections of the clay sculptures, guaranteeing strict quality control under penalty of state punishment.

Paragraph 4. When the soldiers were first arranged in subterranean corridors, they were not the pale, earthy brown statues visitors see in modern museums. Every warrior was painted with brilliant, mineral-based pigments: scarlet cinnabar, green malachite, powdered azurite, and a unique synthetic compound known as Han purple. These vibrant colors were painted directly over a protective base primer layer of natural lacquer, derived from the toxic sap of the Chinese lacquer tree. Preserving this paintwork has posed a formidable challenge for modern conservators. The moment an excavated warrior is exposed to the dry ambient air of northern China, the ancient lacquer dehydrates within minutes. The lacquer layer contracts, curls upwards, and flakes away, irreversibly tearing the delicate mineral paint from the porous terracotta surface.

Paragraph 5. To halt this immediate degradation, scientists partnered with international conservation chemists to formulate protective solutions. Today, freshly unearthed figures are immediately sprayed with an aqueous solution of polyethylene glycol (PEG) or sealed inside airtight plastic enclosures saturated with moisture. Furthermore, metallurgical testing of the polished bronze swords, spears, and halberds held by the warriors demonstrated that their blades had remained remarkably sharp and rust-free over two millennia, preserved by the alkaline chemistry of the surrounding earth. The silent army stands as an enduring monument to the technological prowess and megalithic ambition of ancient China’s foundational dynasty.

groups.title: Questions 8–13
groups.instructions:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?
In boxes 8–13 on your answer sheet, write:
TRUE – if the statement agrees with the information
FALSE – if the statement contradicts the information
NOT GIVEN – if there is no information on this

steps: Đoạn 1 & 2: "...the First Emperor of unified China." / "...the emperor commissioned..."
Đoạn 3: "...torsos, and arms—out of reusable hollow moulds."
Đoạn 3: "...artists individually sculpted unique facial expressions, distinctive hairstyles..."
Đoạn 3: "Master craftsmen stamped their personal names onto hidden sections..."
Đoạn 4: "Every warrior was painted with brilliant, mineral-based pigments..."
Đoạn 4: "...the ancient lacquer dehydrates within minutes. The lacquer layer contracts, curls upwards..."

q8.text: The local farmers immediately recognized that the head they uncovered was over two thousand years old.

steps: Đoạn 1: Nông dân phát hiện thấy đầu tượng bằng đất nung và báo cáo chính quyền, nhưng bài đọc không hề nói họ có biết niên đại hơn 2000 năm tuổi hay không.

q9.text: Construction of Qin Shi Huang’s tomb complex began during his adult years.

steps: Đoạn 2: Bắt đầu xây dựng từ khi còn là thiếu niên ("shortly after ascending the throne as a teenager"), trái ngược với "during his adult years".

q10.text: Each terracotta soldier was given identical facial expressions by the assembly workshops.

steps: Đoạn 3: Mỗi bức tượng được nặn mặt riêng biệt ("individually sculpted unique facial expressions"), mâu thuẫn với "identical".

q11.text: In ancient times, the terracotta warriors were originally displayed without any paint.

steps: Đoạn 4: Ban đầu tượng được sơn màu rực rỡ ("Every warrior was painted with brilliant... pigments"), mâu thuẫn với "without any paint".

q12.text: Chemical solutions are used today to prevent dry air from ruining newly uncovered statues.

steps: Đoạn 5: "Today, freshly unearthed figures are immediately sprayed with an aqueous solution... to halt this immediate degradation".

q13.text: The bronze weapons found in the pits had suffered severe corrosion prior to modern excavation.

steps: Đoạn 5: Vũ khí đồng còn rất sắc bén và không bị gỉ sét ("remained remarkably sharp and rust-free over two millennia"), mâu thuẫn với "severe corrosion".
